title: Unreasonable Leaders Reframe What Is Possible
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay argues against the standard account of leadership as skilled choosing between competing goods. It lays out the familiar either/ors, rural life against a short commute, education against an early career, social good against high profit, and their leadership equivalents, low pay against high morale, flat hierarchy against accountability, clear rules against creativity. Having set them up it refuses them, proposing that the rarer and more consequential move is to hold a view that transcends the trade-off and fuses both ends of the continuum. The word it chooses for this is unreasonable, meaning a refusal to accept conventional wisdom rather than mere stubbornness. The evidence offered is a set of company-building examples treated as instances of the same manoeuvre: Walton on value and cost, Jobs on beauty and function, Winfrey on self-development and the talk show, Bezos on selection and delivery. The closing question is addressed directly to the reader and is the piece's actual ask: name the trade-off you have accepted too readily.
points: The piece's central move is to reject the framing of leadership as skilled choosing, treating the acceptance of a trade-off as often a failure of imagination rather than a sign of realism.
Unreasonable is used in a precise sense, a refusal of received orthodoxy in pursuit of a both/and outcome, not obstinacy or unrealistic demands.
The examples are chosen to show one repeated manoeuvre rather than four separate stories, each fusing two properties the market treated as mutually exclusive.
The explicit list of leadership trade-offs, pay against morale, flat structure against accountability, rules against creativity, gives the reader concrete candidates to test.
The closing question turns the argument into a diagnostic prompt, asking which specific trade-off the reader has stopped interrogating.
quotes: Great leaders are sometimes unreasonable people. They don’t accept the conventional wisdom embraced religiously by others.
To achieve significant breakthroughs, they sometimes reject the accepted orthodoxy and reframe what is possible.
On occasion, a truly remarkable leader will become unreasonable and refuse to compromise.
They will hold a view that transcends trade-offs and seeks to create an outcome fusing two sides of a continuum. They turn either/or into both/and.
Sam Walton built one of the world’s largest businesses by combining high value and low cost.
Jeff Bezos rejected orthodoxy and yoked wide selection with fast delivery, altering how consumers buy products.
